questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(5, -11)$. Which point must lie on the graph of $y = |f(x)|$?

options.why: Reflected across the y-axis instead of taking the absolute value of the output.
Reflected across both the x-axis and the y-axis.
Swapped the x and y coordinates.

questions.solution_text:
For $y = |f(x)|$, the $x$-coordinate is unchanged and the $y$-coordinate is $|-11| = 11$.
Therefore the corresponding point is $(5, 11)$.

questions.question_text: The function $y = f(x)$ has domain $(-\infty, \infty)$ and range $[-5, 12]$. What is the range of $y = |f(x)|$?

options.why: Took the minimum of $|f(x)|$ to be $|-5| = 5$, forgetting that $f$ passes through $0$.
Used the length of the original range, $12 - (-5) = 17$, as the new maximum instead of the larger magnitude.
Made both slips: minimum read as $|-5| = 5$ and maximum read as the range length $12 - (-5) = 17$.

questions.solution_text:
Since $f(x)$ takes all values from $-5$ to $12$, it passes through $0$, so $|f(x)|$ has minimum value $0$.
The maximum value is $\max(|-5|, |12|) = 12$.
Range is $[0, 12]$.

questions.question_text: Which transformation always produces an even function (symmetric across the $y$-axis) for any arbitrary function $y = f(x)$?

options.why: This reflects negative y-values upward and is not generally even unless f is even.
This is a vertical reflection across the x-axis, not an even symmetry.
This is the reciprocal transformation and does not change the parity of f.

questions.solution_text:
Replacing $x$ with $-x$ in $g(x) = f(|x|)$ gives $g(-x) = f(|-x|) = f(|x|) = g(x)$.
Therefore $y = f(|x|)$ is always an **even function**.

questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ is a line with equation $f(x) = 7 - x$. Which statement correctly describes the graph of $y = f(|x|)$?

options.text: A V-shape opening downwards with vertex at $(0, 7)$ and $x$-intercepts at $(\pm 7, 0)$
A V-shape opening upwards with vertex at $(7, 0)$ and $y$-intercept at $(0, 7)$
options.why: This describes y = |f(x)| = |7 - x| rather than y = f(|x|).

options.text: A line with equation y = 7 + x for all real x
options.why: Applied a reflection across the y-axis to the entire domain instead of piecewise |x|.

options.text: A V-shape opening upwards with vertex at $(0, -7)$ and x-intercepts at $(\pm 7, 0)$
options.why: Incorrectly placed the vertex below the x-axis at (0, -7).

questions.solution_text:
$y = 7 - |x|$.
For $x \ge 0$, $y = 7 - x$ with intercepts $(0, 7)$ and $(7, 0)$.
Reflecting across the $y$-axis gives $y = 7 + x$ for $x < 0$, with intercept $(-7, 0)$.
This forms an inverted V-shape with vertex $(0, 7)$ and $x$-intercepts $(\pm 7, 0)$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = f(x)$ has a local minimum at $(6, -3)$ and a local maximum at $(-5, 8)$. What are the turning points of $y = f(|x|)$ for $x > 0$ and $x < 0$?

options.text: Local minimum at $(6, -3)$ and local maximum at $(-5, 8)$
options.why: Retained the turning point from x < 0 which is deleted under y = f(|x|).
Reflected the minimum vertically as in y = |f(x)| rather than horizontally.
Applied inconsistent signs to the mirrored coordinates.

questions.solution_text:
For $y = f(|x|)$, all features for $x < 0$ are discarded.
The local minimum at $(6, -3)$ for $x > 0$ is kept and reflected to $(-6, -3)$.
Local minima at $(6, -3)$ and $(-6, -3)$.

questions.question_text: The parabola $y = f(x) = (x - 4)^2 - 25$ has zeros at $x = -1$ and $x = 9$. Where do sharp corners (cusps) occur on the graph of $y = |f(x)|$?

options.why: Used the axis of symmetry x = 4 instead of the zeros of the function.
Identified the reflected vertex instead of the sharp corners on the x-axis.
Used the y-intercepts rather than the x-intercepts.

questions.solution_text:
Sharp corners on $y = |f(x)|$ occur where the original curve crosses the $x$-axis ($f(x) = 0$ with $f'(x) \neq 0$).
Zeros are $(x - 4)^2 = 25 \implies x - 4 = \pm 5 \implies x = 9$ or $x = -1$.
Sharp corners at $(-1, 0)$ and $(9, 0)$.

questions.question_text: How many real solutions does the equation $|x^2 - 4x - 12| = 7$ have?

options.why: Solved only x^2 - 4x - 12 = 7 and ignored the negative branch x^2 - 4x - 12 = -7.
Assumed the line y = 7 is tangent to the reflected vertex.
Incorrectly evaluated the discriminant to be negative.

questions.solution_text:
The parabola $f(x) = (x - 6)(x + 2)$ has vertex $(2, -16)$ and zeros at $x = -2, 6$.
The graph $y = |x^2 - 4x - 12|$ has local maximum at $(2, 16)$ and cusps at $(-2, 0)$ and $(6, 0)$.
The line $y = 7$ lies strictly between $0$ and $16$, so it intersects the two outer branches and the two reflected inner branches.
Total number of real solutions $= 4$.

questions.question_text: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{x - 2}$ has vertical asymptote $x = 2$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 0$. Which statement accurately describes the asymptotes of $y = f(|x|)$?

options.text: Vertical asymptotes at $x = 2$ and $x = -2$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 0$
Vertical asymptote at $x = 2$ only, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 0$
options.why: Forgot to reflect the vertical asymptote across the y-axis for x < 0.

options.text: Vertical asymptote at $x = 2$ and horizontal asymptote at $y = 3$
options.why: Incorrectly shifted the horizontal asymptote to y = 3.

options.text: Vertical asymptotes at $x = 2$ and $x = -2$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 3$
options.why: Used the numerator value as the horizontal asymptote.

questions.solution_text:
$y = \dfrac{3}{|x| - 2}$.
Vertical asymptotes occur where $|x| - 2 = 0 \implies |x| = 2 \implies x = 2$ and $x = -2$.
As $|x| \to \infty$, $y \to 0$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y = 0$.
